claims.text: The target precursor mixture contains more than five noble-metal elements in near-equiatomic ratios.
Fast heating causes rapid, kinetically driven precursor reduction and uncontrolled nucleation in these noble-metal HEA nanoparticle systems.
Slow, staged heating decouples precursor reduction from nucleation.
Temperature dwells can produce complete, gradual precursor reduction before nucleation begins.
Reduction and initial FCC crystallization can occur simultaneously when mixed metal precursors reduce at the same temperature.
Different noble-metal combinations can form either a single FCC phase or several compositionally distinct FCC phases.
Slow thermal processing permits homogeneous atomic rearrangement under thermodynamically favorable conditions.
Very slow cooling after melting can homogenize single-phase, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Controlling the thermal ramp minimizes local supersaturation.
Controlling the thermal ramp minimizes rapid elemental diffusion.
Reduced local supersaturation and altered diffusion suppress phase separation, elemental segregation, and lattice defects.
Gradual reduction and atomic rearrangement minimize kinetic trapping, local compositional inhomogeneity, and high lattice strain.
Minimizing kinetic trapping promotes uniform nucleation and growth of a single-phase FCC or other desired solid solution.
Staged heating will increase single-phase formation relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Staged heating will reduce elemental segregation relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Staged heating will produce more controlled and uniform nanoparticle morphology relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Staged heating will lower the thermal decomposition temperature relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Rapid heating and cooling typically cause multiple phases, elemental segregation, morphological inhomogeneity, and uncontrolled phase separation through simultaneous reduction and nucleation.
The intervention applies when heating is slow enough to complete precursor reduction before nucleation in more-than-five-element, near-equiatomic noble-metal systems.
Large differences among the reduction kinetics of constituent elements may cause localized deviations from single-phase formation.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator says staged heating minimizes rapid elemental diffusion, whereas the mechanism relies on sufficient atomic rearrangement to remove inhomogeneity and reach a thermodynamically favored solid solution. The intended distinction between suppressing harmful diffusion gradients and enabling homogenizing diffusion is not stated.

The hypothesis requires reduction to be completed before nucleation, but the directly relevant in situ evidence reports complete reduction coinciding with initial alloy crystallization rather than temporally preceding it.
